claim: Cas9 is a prokaryotic CRISPR-associated protein that has been widely adopted as a tool for editing, imaging, and regulating eukaryotic genomes.
source: The prokaryotic CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats)-associated protein, Cas9, has been widely adopted as a tool for editing, imaging, and regulating eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Cas9 applications.

claim: Highly active sgRNAs for Cas9 and dCas9 were found almost exclusively in regions of low nucleosome occupancy.
source: We observed that highly active sgRNAs for Cas9 and dCas9 were found almost exclusively in regions of low nucleosome occupancy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of large-scale genetic screens.

claim: Nucleosomes directly impede Cas9 binding and cleavage in vitro.
source: In vitro experiments demonstrated that nucleosomes in fact directly impede Cas9 binding and cleavage, while chromatin remodeling can restore Cas9 access.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin remodeling can restore Cas9 access to nucleosomal DNA.
source: In vitro experiments demonstrated that nucleosomes in fact directly impede Cas9 binding and cleavage, while chromatin remodeling can restore Cas9 access.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro experiments with chromatin remodeling enzymes.

claim: Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes together with a single chimeric guide RNA provides a programmable endonuclease.
source: Most notably, the CRISPR-associated Cas9 protein from Streptococcus pyogenes, together with a single chimeric guide RNA (sgRNA), provides a programmable endonuclease that has revolutionized our ability to edit genomes (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doudna and Charpentier, 2014.

claim: Cas9 has been modified to a nuclease-dead form (dCas9) to provide a programmable DNA-binding protein that can be fused to effector domains.
source: Cas9 has been further modified to a nuclease-dead form (dCas9) to provide a programmable DNA-binding protein that can be fused to effector domains, making it possible to turn on or off targeted genes, mark specific genomic loci with fluorescent proteins, or alter epigenetic marks (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Qi et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 2013; Maeder et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2015; Hilton et al., 2015; Kearns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing dCas9 applications.

claim: Sequence properties of the target site and sgRNA only partially predict Cas9 activity.
source: While much of the effort to define relevant rules has focused on the sequence of the target site and sgRNA (Chari et al., 2015; Doench et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015), these only partially predict Cas9 activity and suggest that additional determinants likely exist.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on sgRNA design.

claim: CRISPR evolved in archaea and bacteria.
source: CRISPR evolved in archea and bacteria (Makarova et al., 2015) and is likely not optimized to explore and modify large, chromatin-bound eukaryotic genomes, a hypothesis supported by several studies that point to a correlation between rates of DNA binding and cleavage in regions of open chromatin as measured by DNase I hypersensitivity (Chari et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makarova et al., 2015.

claim: CRISPR is likely not optimized to explore and modify large, chromatin-bound eukaryotic genomes.
source: CRISPR evolved in archea and bacteria (Makarova et al., 2015) and is likely not optimized to explore and modify large, chromatin-bound eukaryotic genomes, a hypothesis supported by several studies that point to a correlation between rates of DNA binding and cleavage in regions of open chromatin as measured by DNase I hypersensitivity (Chari et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to studies showing correlation with open chromatin.

claim: There is a correlation between rates of Cas9 DNA binding and cleavage in regions of open chromatin as measured by DNase I hypersensitivity.
source: CRISPR evolved in archea and bacteria (Makarova et al., 2015) and is likely not optimized to explore and modify large, chromatin-bound eukaryotic genomes, a hypothesis supported by several studies that point to a correlation between rates of DNA binding and cleavage in regions of open chromatin as measured by DNase I hypersensitivity (Chari et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chari et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2014.

claim: dCas9 explores euchromatin more frequently than heterochromatin.
source: Additionally, recent single-molecule imaging studies have shown that dCas9 explores euchromatin more frequently than it does heterochromatin (Knight et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2015.

claim: Average CRISPRi activity score shows a robust, periodic pattern with peaks at ~190 bp intervals relative to the TSS.
source: This analysis revealed a robust, periodic pattern of activity, with peaks at ~190 bp intervals relative to the TSS.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of sgRNA activity scores relative to TSS.

claim: The periodicity of CRISPRi activity is highly reminiscent of patterns previously described for nucleosomes.
source: This periodicity was highly reminiscent of patterns previously described for nucleosomes (Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Jiang and Pugh, 2009.

claim: Average nucleosome signal is strongly anti-correlated with CRISPRi activity.
source: Indeed, analysis of K562 MNase-seq data from the ENCODE consortium (Valouev et al., 2011; ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) revealed that the average nucleosome signal was strongly anti-correlated with CRISPRi activity (Figure 1B), suggesting that high nucleosome occupancy leads to low CRISPRi activity.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of MNase-seq data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High nucleosome occupancy leads to low CRISPRi activity.
source: Indeed, analysis of K562 MNase-seq data from the ENCODE consortium (Valouev et al., 2011; ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) revealed that the average nucleosome signal was strongly anti-correlated with CRISPRi activity (Figure 1B), suggesting that high nucleosome occupancy leads to low CRISPRi activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the anti-correlation between nucleosome signal and CRISPRi activity.

claim: Nucleosome phasing is more pronounced in highly expressed genes.
source: To further explore this inverse relationship between CRISPRi activity and nucleosome organization, we exploited the previous observation that nucleosome phasing is more pronounced in highly expressed genes (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valouev et al., 2011.

claim: Peak to trough amplitudes of both CRISPRi activity and nucleosome occupancy are larger for highly expressed genes.
source: In support of a connection, we found that peak to trough amplitudes of both features were larger for highly expressed genes (Figures 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1C and 1D from the analysis of genes grouped by expression.

claim: Almost all highly active sgRNAs target sites with low MNase-seq signal.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that nucleosomes exclude dCas9, almost all of the highly active sgRNAs targeted sites with low MNase-seq signal.
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of individual sgRNAs and their target site nucleosome occupancy.

claim: Not all sgRNAs targeting sites with low nucleosome occupancy are highly active.
source: However, not all sgRNAs targeting sites with low nucleosome occupancy were highly active, matching previous findings that sgRNA and target DNA sequence features also influence efficiency of the CRISPR system (Chari et al., 2015; Doench et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is observed from the data and supported by citations to previous studies on sequence features.

claim: MNase signal, sgRNA length, and sgRNA sequence scoring algorithm each individually correlate with sgRNA activity (p<10-58 for each).
source: We found that each parameter individually correlated with sgRNA activity (p<10-58 for each; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown by linear regression analysis in Figure 1F.

claim: Correction for sequence and length features has minimal impact on the ability of MNase signal to predict CRISPRi activity (p<10-85 after correction).
source: Importantly, correction for sequence and length features had minimal impact on the ability of the MNase signal to predict CRISPRi activity (p<10-85 after correction).
evidence: This is shown by linear regression analysis after correcting for sequence and length features.

claim: A linear fit of MNase signal, sgRNA length, and sequence features provides a stronger correlation with sgRNA activity (p<10-221).
source: Indeed, a linear fit of all three features provided a still stronger correlation (p<10-221; Figure 1F, far right column), suggesting that incorporating nucleosome occupancy in future sgRNA design algorithms could significantly improve predictive value.
evidence: This is shown by linear regression analysis in Figure 1F.

claim: Incorporating nucleosome occupancy in sgRNA design algorithms could significantly improve predictive value.
source: Indeed, a linear fit of all three features provided a still stronger correlation (p<10-221; Figure 1F, far right column), suggesting that incorporating nucleosome occupancy in future sgRNA design algorithms could significantly improve predictive value.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved correlation when nucleosome occupancy is included.

claim: Strong phenotypes from nuclease-active Cas9 were found predominantly in regions of low MNase-seq signal.
source: Analysis of CDS-targeting sgRNAs revealed that strong phenotypes were found predominantly in regions of low MNase-seq signal (Figure 2A), although this relationship was less pronounced than for CRISPRi.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A from the ricin susceptibility screen.

claim: The relationship between nuclease-active Cas9 activity and nucleosome occupancy is less pronounced than for CRISPRi.
source: Analysis of CDS-targeting sgRNAs revealed that strong phenotypes were found predominantly in regions of low MNase-seq signal (Figure 2A), although this relationship was less pronounced than for CRISPRi.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the results for Cas9 and CRISPRi.

claim: Decreased phasing of nucleosomes within the gene body may explain the less pronounced relationship between Cas9 activity and nucleosome occupancy in CDS regions.
source: This may be due to decreased phasing of nucleosomes within the gene body (Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred and supported by citation to Jiang and Pugh, 2009.

claim: The effect of nucleosome position on Cas9 activity is stronger when analyzing all sgRNAs including those targeting cis-regulatory regions.
source: When we analyzed all sgRNAs in the library, thus incorporating information from cis-regulatory regions where nucleosomes are well phased, we found the effect of nucleosome position to be even stronger (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A much stronger correlation with Cas9 phenotypes is obtained when nucleosome occupancy and sgRNA sequence features are both considered.
source: Although nucleosome occupancy was predictive of CRISPR activity independent of sgRNA sequence features, a much stronger correlation was obtained when all features were considered (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by linear regression analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: Nucleosome organization represents an important feature for CRISPR sgRNA design.
source: Therefore, nucleosome organization likely represents an important feature for CRISPR sgRNA design and should be considered a key contributing factor in interpreting future tiling mutagenesis experiments of coding and non-coding regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved predictive power when nucleosome occupancy is considered.

claim: The nucleosome completely protects its DNA from cleavage by Cas9 in vitro.
source: In agreement with our in vivo data, the nucleosome protected its DNA from cleavage by Cas9, and complete protection from cleavage was observed to be independent of target position within the nucleosome (Figures 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro cleavage assays in Figures 3E, 3F and supplementary figures.

claim: Complete protection from Cas9 cleavage by the nucleosome is independent of target position within the nucleosome.
source: In agreement with our in vivo data, the nucleosome protected its DNA from cleavage by Cas9, and complete protection from cleavage was observed to be independent of target position within the nucleosome (Figures 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown by testing multiple PAM sites at different positions within the nucleosome.

claim: Hinz and colleagues reported that Cas9 nuclease activity is inhibited within the nucleosome but not at adjacent linker sequences.
source: While our manuscript was under review, a study by Hinz and colleagues reported a similar in vitro finding that Cas9 nuclease activity is inhibited within the nucleosome but not at adjacent linker sequences (Hinz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hinz et al., 2015.

claim: Nucleosomal DNA undergoes transient unwrapping or breathing at the entry and exit sites, creating a gradient of accessibility along the nucleosome.
source: Additionally, previous single-molecule and biochemical studies have established that nucleosomal DNA undergoes transient unwrapping or breathing at the entry and exit sites, creating a gradient of accessibility along the nucleosome (Li and Widom, 2004; Li et al., 2005; Luger and Hansen, 2005; Choy and Lee, 2012; Tomschik et al., 2009; Polach and Widom, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The cleavage activity of Cas9 in vitro is not detectably influenced by nucleosome breathing.
source: Interestingly, our data suggests that the cleavage activity of Cas9 in vitro is not detectably influenced by this effect, although less stable nucleosomes than the Widom 601 nucleosome or target sites closer to the nucleosome edge may exhibit more breathing and thus more accessibility than those tested here.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing complete protection regardless of position.

claim: Binding by dCas9 is abolished by the presence of the nucleosome, regardless of the targeted dCas9 binding site.
source: Consistent with our cleavage results, binding by dCas9 was abolished by the presence of the nucleosome, regardless of the targeted dCas9 binding site (Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown by electrophoretic mobility shift assays in Figures 4C-E and supplementary figures.

claim: The Cas9 protein poses significant steric clashes with the histones when aligned with nucleosomal DNA.
source: The resulting combined structure reveals that the Cas9 protein poses significant steric clashes with the histones (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by structural alignment in Figure 4F.

claim: It is unlikely that histones and Cas9 could co-occupy the same piece of DNA.
source: Given the extent of overlapping densities in the two structures, it seems unlikely that the histones and Cas9 could co-occupy the same piece of DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing steric clashes.

claim: Binding by Cas9 constitutes melting of target DNA, which may pose an additional barrier to binding on a nucleosome.
source: Additionally, it may be important to note that unlike other DNA binders such as transcription factors, binding by Cas9 constitutes melting of target DNA, which may pose an additional barrier to binding on a nucleosome.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the mechanism of Cas9 binding.

claim: Cas9 is excluded from nucleosomal DNA rather than being capable of displacing histones.
source: This hypothesis leaves two possible outcomes of targeting Cas9 to nucleosomal DNA: either Cas9 is capable of displacing histones in order to engage nucleosomal DNA, or it is excluded altogether. Our data support the latter conclusion.
evidence: This is concluded from the binding and cleavage data showing no activity on nucleosomal DNA.

claim: yChd1 mediates nucleosome sliding in an ATP-dependent manner without additional co-factors.
source: To recapitulate the effects of chromatin remodeling in vitro, we used a purified, truncated form of the Snf2-like chromatin remodeling enzyme Chd1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yChd1), which had previously been shown to mediate nucleosome sliding in an ATP-dependent manner without additional co-factors (Patel et al., 2011; 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patel et al., 2011; 2013.

claim: Addition of yChd1 results in a shift toward lower molecular weight bands in HaeIII digestion, indicative of diminished protection at HaeIII sites.
source: Upon addition of yChd1, we observed a shift toward lower molecular weight bands, indicative of dimished protection at HaeIII sites while still maintaining an overall chromatinized state (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by the restriction enzyme accessibility assay in Figure 5D.

claim: Sites within the 601 nucleosome are strongly protected from cleavage by Cas9 before addition of remodeler.
source: Before addition of the remodeler to our chromatinized plasmid, we found that sites within the 601 nucleosome were strongly protected from cleavage by Cas9, consistent with our mononucleosome results (Figure 5E-G, PAM sites without remodeler).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5E-G for the chromatinized plasmid system.

claim: When the 601 nucleosome is remodeled by yChd1, Cas9 cleavage efficiency is restored to around 80% of the corresponding naked plasmid control.
source: However, when the 601 nucleosome was remodeled by yChd1, as indicated by a loss of protection from restriction enzyme cleavage (approaching protection levels similar to those in the linker region), Cas9 cleavage efficiency was restored to around 80% of the corresponding naked plasmid control (Figures 5E–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5E-G by comparing cleavage with and without remodeler.

claim: The decrease in protection along the 601 sequence upon addition of yChd1 is mediated by the nucleosome displacement activity of yChd1 rather than by a non-specific effect on cleavage efficiency.
source: Notably, the percent protection at the EcoRI site adjacent to the positioned nucleosome did not decrease upon addition of yChd1, demonstrating that the decrease in protection along the 601 sequence was mediated by the nucleosome displacement activity of yChd1 rather than by a non-specific effect on cleavage efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control showing no change at the adjacent EcoRI site.

claim: Chromatin remodeling provides a potential mechanism by which Cas9 may efficiently modify broad portions of eukaryotic genomes.
source: While our data with the chromatinized plasmid system confirm our findings that a well-positioned nucleosome provides a profound block to Cas9 cleavage, our further finding that chromatin remodeling restores access to nucleosomal DNA provides one potential mechanism by which Cas9 may efficiently modify broad portions of eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing restored access after remodeling.

claim: The nucleosome effectively reduces the size of the eukaryotic genome available to Cas9.
source: By masking ~147 bp of DNA, the nucleosome effectively reduces the size of the eukaryotic genome available to Cas9.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that nucleosomes block Cas9 access.

claim: Off-target binding by Cas9 at PAM plus seed sequences more frequently occurs in regions of open chromatin.
source: Previous studies using ChIP-seq to assay Cas9 binding have shown that off-target binding at PAM plus seed sequences more frequently occurs in regions of open chromatin (Wu et al., 2014; O'Geen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2014; O'Geen et al., 2015.

claim: The discrete pattern of nucleosome organization is able to modulate the efficiency of Cas9 binding and cleavage at on-target sites.
source: Our data expand upon these findings to show that the discrete pattern of nucleosome organization is able to modulate the efficiency of Cas9 binding and cleavage at on-target sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the in vivo and in vitro data presented.

claim: Accounting for nucleosome occupancy offers a significant improvement in predictive power for sgRNA design.
source: The practical implications of these observations are underscored by our finding that accounting for nucleosome occupancy offers a significant improvement in predictive power for sgRNA design.
evidence: This is shown by the linear regression analysis demonstrating improved correlation.

claim: Transient displacement of nucleosomes occurs during replication, remodeling, and transcription.
source: While our data show that nucleosomes strongly protect their DNA from Cas9 binding and cleavage in vitro, their organization in cells is not static. Transient displacement of nucleosomes occurs during replication, remodeling, and transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleosome dynamics.

claim: Despite brief exposure of nucleosomal DNA during remodeling and various cellular processes, there is still a clear anti-correlation between Cas9 activity and nucleosome occupancy in vivo.
source: However, despite brief exposure of nucleosomal DNA during remodeling and various other cellular processes, we still observe a clear anti-correlation between Cas9 activity and nucleosome occupancy in vivo, suggesting that the barrier to Cas9 target recognition exists even in a cellular environment.
evidence: This is observed from the in vivo data despite the dynamic nature of nucleosomes.

claim: The barrier to Cas9 target recognition exists even in a cellular environment.
source: However, despite brief exposure of nucleosomal DNA during remodeling and various other cellular processes, we still observe a clear anti-correlation between Cas9 activity and nucleosome occupancy in vivo, suggesting that the barrier to Cas9 target recognition exists even in a cellular environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistent anti-correlation observed in vivo.

claim: The balance between nucleosome disruption, turnover, and repositioning in the cell leads to the average level of occupancy and positioning at each site observed by MNase-seq.
source: Indeed, the balance between nucleosome disruption, turnover, and repositioning in the cell leads to the average level of occupancy and positioning at each site observed by MNase-seq (Valouev et al., 2011; Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Valouev et al., 2011; Jiang and Pugh, 2009.

claim: It is likely the overall effect of average nucleosome positioning that leads to the observed anti-correlation with Cas9/sgRNA activity.
source: Thus, our data suggest that it is likely the overall effect of this average nucleosome positioning that leads to the observed anti-correlation with Cas9/sgRNA activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between MNase-seq data and Cas9 activity.

claim: There is likely a fundamental difference between applications that use dCas9 versus nuclease-active Cas9.
source: Additionally, it is important to note that there is likely a fundamental difference between applications that use dCas9 versus nuclease-active Cas9.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the different requirements for dCas9 and Cas9.

claim: Knock-down of transcription by CRISPRi likely requires persistent binding by dCas9 to continually block transcription.
source: Knock-down of transcription by CRISPRi likely requires persistent binding by dCas9 to continually block transcription, and would be largely ineffective during S-phase when transcription is globally shut down.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of CRISPRi.

claim: CRISPRi would be largely ineffective during S-phase when transcription is globally shut down.
source: Knock-down of transcription by CRISPRi likely requires persistent binding by dCas9 to continually block transcription, and would be largely ineffective during S-phase when transcription is globally shut down.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on cell cycle biology.

claim: To make a genomic edit, Cas9 must succeed in cleaving DNA only once.
source: In contrast, to make a genomic edit, Cas9 must succeed in cleaving DNA only once, and could potentially take advantage of nucleosome turnover during replication.
evidence: This is reasoning about the mechanism of genome editing by Cas9.

claim: Cas9 could potentially take advantage of nucleosome turnover during replication.
source: In contrast, to make a genomic edit, Cas9 must succeed in cleaving DNA only once, and could potentially take advantage of nucleosome turnover during replication.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about how Cas9 might access DNA during replication.

claim: Nucleosome position and occupancy will be of particular concern to applications that use nuclease-dead Cas9 and require sustained binding.
source: We expect, however, that nucleosome position and occupancy will be of particular concern to applications that use the nuclease-dead Cas9 and require sustained binding.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings.

claim: Nucleosome organization represents only one aspect of eukaryotic chromatin.
source: Furthermore, nucleosome organization represents only one aspect of eukaryotic chromatin, and thus, our results contribute a first step in understanding and exploiting how chromatin affects Cas9 activity to enable more sophisticated and precise rules for targeting Cas9.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the broader context of chromatin structure.

claim: The results contribute a first step in understanding and exploiting how chromatin affects Cas9 activity.
source: Furthermore, nucleosome organization represents only one aspect of eukaryotic chromatin, and thus, our results contribute a first step in understanding and exploiting how chromatin affects Cas9 activity to enable more sophisticated and precise rules for targeting Cas9.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claim: The K562 dCas9-KRAB-BFP cell line tested negative for mycoplasma.
source: The resulting cell line tested negative for mycoplasma (MycoAlert Kit, Lonza, Basel, Switzerland) in regular screenings, and cytogenetic profiling by array comparative genomic hybridization (not shown) closely matched previous characterizations of the K562 cell line (Naumann et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a quality control measure reported in the methods.

claim: Cytogenetic profiling of the K562 dCas9-KRAB-BFP cell line closely matched previous characterizations of the K562 cell line.
source: The resulting cell line tested negative for mycoplasma (MycoAlert Kit, Lonza, Basel, Switzerland) in regular screenings, and cytogenetic profiling by array comparative genomic hybridization (not shown) closely matched previous characterizations of the K562 cell line (Naumann et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naumann et al., 2001.

claim: The 601 sequence contains numerous NGG protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs) required for Cas9 recognition, spanning the full length of the DNA at different helical positions.
source: Conveniently, the 601 sequence contains numerous NGG protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs) required for Cas9 recognition, spanning the full length of the DNA at different helical positions, allowing us to test the effects of position and solvent accesibility within the nucleosome (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and described in the text.

claim: The 601 sequence allows testing of the effects of position and solvent accessibility within the nucleosome on Cas9 activity.
source: Conveniently, the 601 sequence contains numerous NGG protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs) required for Cas9 recognition, spanning the full length of the DNA at different helical positions, allowing us to test the effects of position and solvent accesibility within the nucleosome (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is the rationale for using the 601 sequence in the experiments.

claim: Modifications introduced by Cas9 can disrupt cis-regulatory regions.
source: We observed phenotypes consistent with the expected knockdown phenotype primarily in coding sequences (CDS) but also in some promoter regions, consistent with recent results showing that modifications introduced by Cas9 can disrupt cis-regulatory regions (Canver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Canver et al., 2015.

claim: A comprehensive algorithm for predicting highly active CRISPRi sgRNAs that accounts for nucleosome occupancy shows greater correlation with the dataset (cross-validation R2=0.32).
source: We have recently developed a comprehensive algorithm for predicting highly active CRISPRi sgRNAs that, by accounting for nucleosome occupancy, higher order sequence features, and non-linear relationships in these parameters, shows even greater correlation with this dataset that was already enriched for active sgRNAs using our original CRISPRi library design principles (Gilbert et al., 2014) (cross-validation R2=0.32; Horlbeck et al., manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is a reference to work in preparation showing improved prediction.
